title: Latin and Greek: Where the Parts Come From
short: Many English words come from Latin, often by way of French, and many learned and scientific words come from Greek.
trouble: Learners treat all roots as Latin. ph, ch (said like k), y and th inside a root are clues to Greek (philanthropist, chronic, synchronize, pathos); some words even mix the two languages.

blocks.html: English borrowed a huge number of words from Latin, the language of ancient Rome. Many came through French, which grew out of Latin. English also borrowed from ancient Greek, especially for ideas, science and learning. So two parts can mean the same thing: Latin uni- and Greek mono- both mean “one” (a unicycle and a monorail each have one of something).

blocks.html: Clues that a part is Greek: ph said like f (philanthropist), ch said like k (chronic), y used as a vowel (synchronize, polymath) and th (pathos, hypothesis). Latin parts make up most everyday long words: credible, conspicuous, intermittent.

Knowing which language a part comes from helps in two ways. First, it tells you which partner part to expect: Greek parts tend to join other Greek parts (philanthropist is all Greek). Second, it helps with look-alike parts: Greek a- means “without” in apathy, but the a- in English asleep means “on.”

blocks.title: Latin or Greek?
blocks.q: Is telepathy built from Latin or from Greek parts?
steps: Look for clues in the spelling: th and a y used as a vowel both point to Greek.
Both tele and path are Greek parts, so the word is Greek through and through: “feeling from far away.”
blocks.a: Greek. Telepathy is the supposed sending of thoughts from one mind to another without words.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: a person who gives money or time to help others
entry.ex: A local {philanthropist} paid for new books in every classroom.
entry.ctx: Though she had grown rich selling furniture, the {philanthropist} lived simply and gave most of her money to hospitals and schools.
entry.etym: From Greek philanthropos, “loving people”: philein (to love) + anthropos (human being).

mn.cue: PHIL loves ANTHROPOS: Phil loves people
mn.text: Phil loves people so much that he pays for a brand-new park where everyone in town can play: Phil is a {philanthropist}.

scene.alt: Children cheer a smiling man named Phil under a banner thanking him for a new playground.

blocks.html: Treating every root as Latin. The clues ph, ch said like k, y and th point to Greek (philanthropist, chronic, synchronize, pathos). And some words mix the two languages: television joins Greek tele (far) to Latin vision (seeing), and automobile joins Greek auto (self) to Latin mobile (moving).
Spelling clues are hints, not rules. Phone and photo are Greek, but a word like shepherd has a p-h made of two separate sounds and is plain English. Use the clue together with the meaning.
